text:
I created a P6 baseline schedule with an AI coding agent. It did the typing. It did not do the planning.

This was live work: a new resource-loaded baseline for an EPC package, built with Claude Code. Project and client names are removed, and the charts in the images show shares and indices, not real quantities. This is how it went:

1. Inputs. The contract key dates, the BOQ with quantities and manhour norms per cost code, the client's drawing and material delivery dates, and my construction sequence.

2. Baseline. It built WBS, activities, logic and calendars as a model in code, then wrote the XER that I imported into P6 as a new project: 281 activities, 664 relationships, no constraints, no negative lags.

3. Loading. Every activity got quantity × norm from the BOQ. P6 manhours matched the BOQ on all 106 cost codes.

4. Curves. Custom P6 resource curves first. Then weekly and monthly S-curves, commodity curves (piping, excavation, concrete, steel, equipment, cable) and manpower histograms, all from the same loaded schedule.

5. DCMA 14. An automated check on every revision. On the next schedule I built this way, the first run passed 5 checks and the final revision passed 8. Four fail, and the report lists every activity behind them.

6. Cross-check. An independent scheduler recalculated every date and float before I pressed F9 in P6.

Revision 6 was issued on the third day.

Where it went wrong:
• It started piping erection too early. I had to give it the real monthly production plan.
• Its own checks caught two errors before the files reached me: numbers written in a format P6 would not import, and a concrete quantity that was not in the BOQ.
• It built one manpower plan from a stale file with old manhours.

What it flagged for my decision:
• One contract key date could not be met with the client's own delivery date.
• One DCMA check could be passed by spreading manhours onto activities that have none in the BOQ. It did not do that.

The sequence, the production rates, what the client will accept and what is true on site are still my job.

So, a question for planners and project controls people. If an AI agent can build the baseline, load it, draw the curves and audit it, what is the planning engineer's job in five years?

A. Reviewer of AI output
B. Fewer planners, each covering more projects
C. More valuable than ever, because judgement is what remains
D. Something else

Comment your letter and why. I will read every answer.

#ProjectControls #Planning #PrimaveraP6 #AI #ClaudeCode #DCMA14 #EPC #Scheduling

images.alt: Workflow card: how a resource-loaded P6 baseline was created with an AI coding agent. Inputs, six steps from read to cross-check with the planner's decision at each step, and the result: 281 activities, 664 relationships, 106 cost codes reconciled, 146 client deliverables tracked, 0 constraints.

DCMA 14-point check, first run against final revision: checks passed went from 5 to 8 and failed from 7 to 4. High float, negative float and the critical path test now pass. Lags, finish-to-start share, long activities and activities with no manhours still fail.
Two bar charts. Piping erection plan by month before and after a back-loaded P6 resource curve, and direct manpower by month before and after monthly production targets, shown as shares and an index.
